_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: That was said in the presence of three: if the owner [of the information] said it before three, one who reveals it is not speaking malicious speech, since the owner showed his mind from the start that he does not mind if it is revealed. For he surely knew that it would end up revealed, as “your friend has a friend”: this one reveals it to his friend and that one to his friend, until it is known.
tosafot:a1.1: Any matter that was said in the presence of three has no malicious speech in it: that is, a matter like “There is fire at so-and-so’s home” [15b], which can be understood as not said as malicious speech. But if he said something provocative against his fellow, even if he said it in his presence, it is malicious speech.
gershom:a1.1: Any matter that was said in the presence of three: when the first one said it before three, if one of them goes back and tells it, there is no malicious speech in it, since he said it before three knowingly, not minding if the matter becomes public, as “your friend has a friend,” and so on.
rashi:a2.1: He that blesses his friend with a loud voice … it shall be counted a curse to him: that blessing is a curse to him, to his friend [the host].
rashi:a2.2: And people hear: violent people hear that he is rich, and they go and extort his money. Another version: they afflict him, in that guests come to lodge with him until they use up his money.
gershom:a2.1: And people hear and afflict him: the authorities.
gershom:a3.1: And they afflict him: for they say, he is surely rich, since he spends so much.
rashi:a3.1: He will come to speak of him in a derogatory manner: for when he tells of his goodness too much, he himself says “except for this bad trait in him,” or others hear him praising and say, “But doesn’t he have such-and-such a trait?”
gershom:a4.1: For through his goodness he comes to speak of his bad side: for they look into him and say to him: The one you praise so much, didn’t we hear that he did such-and-such?
gershom:a5.1: There are those who say: it was not stated as a teaching, but there was an incident of this kind. [A note in the printed edition adds that a comment seems to belong further on, at “Be content [ho’el], take two talents,” explaining that ho’el means an oath: to swear.]
rashi:a5.1: Stinginess [literally, narrowness of the eye]: his eye is narrow toward others, and he does not let his neighbors benefit from his utensils by lending them.
rashi:a6.1: Him I will destroy: and we established above [15b] that this means leprous marks.
rashi:a7.1: Let there not fail from the house of Joab: because he killed Abner.
rashi:a8.1: Ho’el: swear that Elisha sent you, and take the talents.
rashi:a10.1: But when he was strong his heart became arrogant, and so on: the passage speaks of Uzziah.
tosafot:a10.1: But when he was strong his heart became arrogant, and so on: this is written of Uzziah. In Chronicles it is written: “And Johanan begot Azariah; he it is who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem” (I Chronicles 5). This needs study: why is “who served as priest” written of him more than of the others? For it lists there all the High Priests who served in the First Temple, and it lists several priests before him; why then is “who served as priest” written of Azariah more than of the others? One can say: because when Uzziah came [to burn the incense], he put himself forward to contend for the priesthood more than the others [see II Chronicles 26:17–18].
rashi:a12.1: Who treated his house as exclusively his: his household utensils, which he did not lend to others.
gershom:a6.1: One whose house is exclusively his: who wants to enjoy alone all the good he has in his house and does not want others to enjoy it with him.
rashi:a13.1: Why was it juxtaposed, and so on: in the portion of Ve’ata Tetzaveh, the matter of the inauguration offerings is juxtaposed to the priestly vestments. [Rashi thus places the juxtaposition in Exodus 28–29, not in Leviticus as the English gloss on the daf has it.]
rashi:a13.2: And they dipped the coat in the blood: it was a hint for them that atonement for blood would come about through a tunic.
gershom:a7.1: And they dipped the coat in the blood: a sign: let the tunic come and atone for an act of blood.
gershom:a8.1: Let an item that is at a height come: the mitre, which was on the head.
tosafot:a14.1: The belt atones for thought of the heart, where it is: the belt is like a very long girdle of fine linen, and it is also found in the Midrash that the priest would wind it around himself twice, opposite a person’s heart.
gershom:a9.1: Where it is: for he would gird it opposite his heart, as it is written: “They shall not gird themselves with anything that causes sweat” (Ezekiel 44:18), [that is, not] in a place where one sweats, such as under the armpits, but opposite his heart, where one does not sweat.
rashi:a15.1: Without ephod or teraphim: at a time when there is no ephod, there is the sin of teraphim.
gershom:a10.1: Without ephod [or teraphim]: that is to say, there is no ephod to atone for the sin of teraphim.
rashi:a15.2: That produces sound: the bells of the robe are heard, [and atone] for an act of sound, malicious speech. And you said that leprous marks come for it!
gershom:a11.1: An item that produces sound: as it is written: “And its sound shall be heard when he goes in” (Exodus 28:35). Evidently one who speaks malicious speech has atonement through the robe and is not struck with leprosy.
rashi:a17.1: Where his actions were effective: that people quarreled because of him. And if you ask: why did the Gemara not object to him from bloodshed and forbidden relations, for which it said above that leprous marks come, while here it teaches that the priestly vestments atone? The answer is that this teaching, that the priestly vestments atone, is not for the sinner himself but for the others who are punished on his account. For of bloodshed it is written: “For blood pollutes [the land]” (Numbers 35:33), and of forbidden relations it is written: “And the land became impure, and I visited its iniquity upon it” (Leviticus 18:25). But with malicious speech we do not find that others are punished for it.
tosafot:a17.1: In brief: Tosafot quotes Rashi’s explanation in full: where his actions were effective, people quarreled because of him; and the Gemara does not raise bloodshed and forbidden relations, for which leprous marks also come, because the vestments atone for those sins only for the others punished on their account (“For blood pollutes,” Numbers 35:33; “And the land became impure, and I visited its iniquity upon it,” Leviticus 18:25), whereas for malicious speech others are not punished. Tosafot objects that this does not seem right: Shevuot 39a says that others are punished for every transgression when it was in their power to protest, and when it was not, not even for forbidden relations and bloodshed. The Ri answers that bloodshed poses no difficulty at all, since it carries a court-imposed death penalty and the priestly vestments atone for [the sin that carries] death, yet leprous marks still come upon him. Others explain that the Gemara’s answer, “where his actions were effective, where they were not effective,” applies to bloodshed and forbidden relations as well: actually killing is “effective,” and the vestments do not atone for it but leprous marks come upon him; “not effective” is, for example, shaming one’s fellow in public, which counts as shedding blood (Bava Metzia 58b), and for that the vestments atone. Likewise, actual forbidden relations are “effective,” and “not effective” is like what is said in Shabbat 55b: since they delayed the women’s bird offerings, Scripture regards them as though they had lain with them. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a19.1: That is in private: the incense is offered in the Sanctuary in private, as taught in chapter Hotziu Lo of tractate Yoma (44a): they withdraw from between the Entrance Hall and the altar at the time of the burning of the incense. And malicious speech is done in private.
gershom:a12.1: Let an item that is in private come: the incense, which he would offer inside the Sanctuary, where no one is permitted to enter to see it, and let it atone for a private act, malicious speech, which people speak in private and in inner rooms.
rashi:a20.1: Bloodshed is difficult, and so on: for we said above that the priestly vestments atone for others [Rashi on 16a, above], and we see that the heifer whose neck is broken atones for others, since for the killer it does not atone, as we hold in Sota (47b): if the heifer’s neck was broken and afterward the killer was found, from where do we know that he is executed? The verse states: “And no atonement can be made for the land,” and so on (Numbers 35:33).
rashi:a20.2: Malicious speech is difficult: with what was taught above, that the priestly vestments atone.
gershom:a13.1: Bloodshed is difficult with bloodshed: for there you said that the tunic atones, and here you said that the heifer whose neck is broken atones.
rashi:a21.1: Where it is not known who killed him: the heifer atones.
gershom:a14.1: Where it is known who killed him: the tunic atones.
rashi:a22.1: He is deserving of death: and as long as he has not been put to death, the others have no atonement, as it is written: “And no atonement can be made for the land,” and so on (Numbers 35:33).
gershom:a15.1: Intentionally, but they did not warn him: so he is not liable to death; the tunic atones.
rashi:a23.1: In private: for a private act, the incense atones.
gershom:a16.1: This in private, that in public: for malicious speech spoken in private, the incense atones, like the privacy [of the incense]. [A note in the printed edition: it seems the heading should read “That where his actions were not effective,” and so on; Rabbeinu explains that this answer applies to bloodshed as well, as Tosafot also write here in the name of “others explain.”] Where his actions were not actually effective, but he did something, for example he shamed his fellow, of whom we say it is regarded as though he killed him; or a matter of forbidden relations, as we say of the sons of Eli: Scripture regards them as though they had lain with [such women]: the robe atones.
gershom:a17.1: And that, in public: the robe atones, like “and its sound shall be heard.”
rashi:b1.1: In public: since it is an act of sound, the robe atones.
rashi:b2.1: He separated: for it was over malicious speech that leprous marks came upon him.
gershom:b1.1: He separated between husband and wife: for he caused them to quarrel through the malicious speech he spoke between them.
rashi:b3.1: Chatter [patit]: a word for a sound that goes out quietly; (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b3.2: He is to bring an offering of chatter: for birds cry out all the time.
gershom:b2.1: An act of chatter: he chattered and made his voice heard in malicious speech.
gershom:b3.1: Therefore he is to bring an offering of chatter: birds, which make their voices heard all the time.
rashi:b4.1: One might have thought: do not hit him: over a matter that calls for rebuke.
rashi:b4.2: Slap him: with the back of the hand.
gershom:b4.1: One might have thought: that is, that “You shall not hate” means that he should not hit him, and so on.
rashi:b5.1: And his face changes: that he rebukes him in public, so as to make his face blanch.
gershom:b5.1: One might have thought, even if his face changes: the face of the one rebuked, for example if he rebukes him in front of many.
gershom:b6.1: Do not bear sin because of him: that you not shame him.
rashi:b6.1: Splinter: that is to say, [if one says to him: remove] the small sin in your hand, this one can say to him: Remove, you, the great sin in your hand. Therefore they cannot rebuke, since they are all sinners.
rashi:b6.2: Who knows how to rebuke: respectfully, so that his face does not change.
gershom:b7.1: If there is anyone in this generation who can rebuke: that is to say, even the good ones spoil their deeds and cannot rebuke others; for if one says to his fellow, “Remove the splinter from between your teeth” [the printed text is corrected here from “eyes”], he can answer him, “Remove the beam from between your eyes.”
gershom:b8.1: Who knows how to rebuke: for example, so that the face of the one rebuked does not change.
gershom:b9.1: Who can receive rebuke: for if, in this generation, one rebukes a person, he immediately hates him.
rashi:b7.1: I would complain about him: when I saw something unseemly in him.
rashi:b8.1: Rebuke for its own sake: for the sake of Heaven.
rashi:b8.2: And humility not for its own sake: that he makes himself humble and does not want to rebuke him, and that humility is not for the sake of Heaven but so that the other will not hate him.
rashi:b8.3: As the Master says: in the first chapter of tractate Avoda Zara (20b): Humility is the greatest of them all, as it is written: “Because the Lord has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble” (Isaiah 61:1); it does not say “to the pious.”
tosafot:b8.1: And humility not for its own sake: that he makes himself humble and does not want to rebuke him, and that humility is not for the sake of Heaven but so that the other will not hate him. And some explain humility not for its own sake as [humility] out of pride, or so that people will say, “He is a humble man, who lowers himself and stays silent when he is reviled and insulted,” not for the sake of Heaven but to make a name for himself. But the Kuntres [Rashi], who explained humility not for its own sake as withholding rebuke from those who need it, does not seem right to me, for that is a completely wicked person.
rashi:b9.1: [Ḥiyya bar Rav] said to him [Rashi’s heading reads “Rabbi Ḥiyya”]: to Shmuel: “See, Master, that Rav Huna is distressing us,” in that he strikes and beats me.
rashi:b9.2: When he left: when Ḥiyya bar Rav left, Rav Huna said to Shmuel: This is why I distress him, because he does such-and-such disgraceful things. And this is humility not for its own sake, for he did not say it to his face, and behind his back he spoke of his disgrace.
tosafot:b9.1: Heaven forbid that the seed of Rav should be humiliated because of me: and this is humility not for its own sake, for he refrained from shaming him because of his father’s honor.
gershom:b10.1: As the Master says: Humility is the greatest of them all: as taught in tractate Avoda Zara (20b) [the printed text corrects “Ketubot”]: Rabbi [a name, “Naḥum,” is marked for deletion] says: Alacrity brings one to cleanliness, and so on, up to: humility is the greatest of them all, as it is written: “The spirit of the Lord is upon me,” and so on.
gershom:b11.1: After he left: Ḥiyya bar Rav.
gershom:b12.1: He said to him: Rav Huna said to Shmuel: This is what he was doing to me.
gershom:b13.1: Heaven forbid that the seed of Rav should be humiliated because of me: and this is humility not for its own sake. For it would have been better had he said it to his face, in order to rebuke him, and that would have been rebuke for its own sake, than not saying it to his face and saying it behind him.
rashi:b10.1: Until where: is a person obligated to rebuke his fellow?
rashi:b10.2: Until hitting: until this one grows angry and hits the one rebuking.
rashi:b10.3: Until cursing: until he curses the one rebuking. Jonathan rebuked Saul until Saul grew angry.
gershom:b14.1: Until where is rebuke: that is, up to what point is he obligated not to refrain from rebuking his fellow?
gershom:b15.1: Until hitting: until the one rebuked hits him, as if to say: I do not want your rebuke.
gershom:b16.1: Until cursing: or until the one rebuked curses him.
gershom:b17.1: Or until reprimand: until the one rebuked scolds him.
gershom:b18.1: Then Saul’s anger was kindled: Saul was the one rebuked and Jonathan the one rebuking.
gershom:b19.1: Then Saul’s anger was kindled: that is reprimand, for he reprimanded him.
gershom:b20.1: He subjected himself to more: for he was exempt from rebuking him from the moment [Saul] reprimanded him.
tosafot:b13.1: But according to the one who says: Until reprimand, aren’t hitting and cursing written? And if you say: according to the one who says cursing, too, isn’t hitting written? One can say: perhaps as the Gemara answers, it was due to Jonathan’s fondness [for David]. Alternatively, he does not expound the verse “And Saul cast,” since it is not part of this verse, “Then Saul’s anger was kindled,” but is a different verse.
rashi:b14.1: Until hitting: the host hits the guest or his wife.
rashi:b14.2: Until he packs: the host packs the guest’s things on his back, to throw them out of the house.
gershom:b21.1: Until where should a person not change his lodging: that is, how much must the guest bear from his host before leaving his house?
gershom:b22.1: Until hitting: until the host hits him, as if to say: Leave my house.
gershom:b23.1: Until he packs his things on his back: that he puts his things on his staff and places them on his neck, to put him out of his house.
rashi:b15.1: With packing, and with hitting the guest himself, everyone agrees that he can no longer stay. Shmuel holds: since he does not hit him himself, what difference does it make to him? Therefore [he stays] until packing. [Rashi thus gives this reason to Shmuel; the English on the daf gives it to Rav.]
gershom:b24.1: With hitting him himself: if he hits the guest himself, everyone agrees that he certainly may leave.
gershom:b25.1: Hitting his wife: the guest’s wife.
gershom:b26.1: He will come to fight: to quarrel with the host over why he hit his wife.
rashi:b16.1: And why is it so: [why must] he bear so much?
rashi:b16.2: A guest: who changes his lodging.
rashi:b16.4: And is degraded: himself, for people say: How difficult these two are, that they could not live together.
gershom:b27.1: And why is it so: that is, why must he bear so much before he leaves?
gershom:b28.1: As the Master says: A guest degrades and is degraded: if he changes his lodging, people will say the host is unpleasant, since the guest could not bear him; and they will also degrade the guest and say he was unpleasant, since he did not bear with the host.
gershom:b29.1: To the place where his tent had been: from here [we learn] that he returned to the lodging he had been in at first.
rashi:b18.1: On his journeys: on the road where he used to camp from journey to journey, for he did not change his lodging places.
rashi:b18.2: A temporary lodging: for example, a guest on the road who lodged there merely by chance, because the sun set on him there. According to the one who says “his tent,” only a fixed lodging counts; according to the one who says “his journeys,” even a temporary one counts.
gershom:b30.1: And he went on his journeys: on those journeys he had gone on at first.
gershom:b31.1: A temporary lodging: where a person does not regularly stay, but it happened to him for the moment: [the question is] whether he must make it his fixed lodging. According to the one who says “his journeys,” [this means] regular journeys, but not a temporary one. [Rashi reads the difference the other way.]
gershom:b32.1: “And King Solomon sent”: this is written in Kings. And in Chronicles it is written: “The son of a woman,” and so on, for his mother’s father was from Dan; evidently he held on [to the craft of his fathers].
gershom:b33.1: And his father was of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father’s mother was from Dan, as it is written in Chronicles: “The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan.” And he held on to the craft of his fathers, from his father’s side and his mother’s.
tosafot:b19.1: A person should never change from the craft of his father and the craft of his fathers: and it brings a proof that his mother was of the children of Dan, and he took up for himself the craft of his forefathers.
tosafot:b19.2: This is how we read it: “As the Master says: His mother was from Dan and his father from Naphtali,” for in Chronicles (II Chronicles 2) it is written that his mother was of the children of Dan.
rashi:b21.1: The limit of suffering: the end of the measure of suffering, that is, suffering than which there is none smaller.
rashi:b21.2: And it does not suit him: it is not made to his measure properly, and it is a distress to him.
rashi:b21.3: To dilute: a cup of wine with hot water.
gershom:b34.1: Until where is the limit of suffering: that is, how small a distress counts as suffering, so that if it happens to him within forty days he has atonement and has not received his World here.
gershom:b35.1: And it does not suit him: it is not the size of his body, either too small or too large; this is suffering.
rashi:b22.1: His cloak turns around: he did not put it on in the right way, and he must turn it over and take it off.
gershom:b36.1: His cloak turns around: at the moment he sought to put it on.
gershom:b37.1: To take three, and two came up: for he must take more trouble and reach his hand in a second time to take the third.
rashi:b23.1: Three, and two came up in his hand: there is the exertion of going back and taking a third.
rashi:b24.1: And why is it so: that is, for what halakhic purpose do we need to know what counts as suffering?
rashi:b24.2: Has received his World: all his repose that awaits him in the future [he has received here]. And if one of these things happens to him, that is suffering.
gershom:b38.1: And why is it so: why do I need to be precise about the limit of suffering?
